thinking_and_logic: The submitted implementation does not include the logic to find a pair; it iterates with an empty loop body and returns a constant answer. The canonical reasoning for this problem is: as you scan the array, for each element x at index i, compute complement c = target - x; if c has been seen before at index j, return [j, i]. This guarantees not using the same element twice (because you only match with earlier indices) and achieves linear time.
code_assessment: Compared to the answer key, the final code is missing both the brute-force nested-loop check and the optimal one-pass hash-map technique. The hardcoded return matches the documented pitfall (“Hardcoding the answer to the visible example”) and explains the failures like “pair at end” and “negative numbers,” since the output never depends on input. Implementing the one-pass hash map would make the solution correct across placements and values while meeting the O(n) time requirement for up to 1e5 elements.

next_steps.action: Implement Two Sum using the one-pass hash map pattern (seen value -> index; check complement before inserting).
next_steps.why: It is the canonical optimal solution (O(n) time) and directly prevents using the same element twice by construction.
next_steps.how: Write: `seen = {}`; loop `i, x in enumerate(nums)`; `c = target - x`; if `c in seen: return [seen[c], i]`; else `seen[x] = i`; return `[]` only if required by the platform.

next_steps.action: Practice writing a correct brute-force solution first, then optimizing.
next_steps.why: It ensures you always have a working answer under interview pressure, and then you can improve complexity.
next_steps.how: Start with double loop returning on `nums[i] + nums[j] == target` (i<j), run through 2-3 manual examples, then refactor to the hash map approach.
